name: Hydrogen
fact: The lightest and most abundant element — about 75% of the visible universe's mass.

name: Helium
fact: The second-lightest element; it never freezes at normal pressure and lifts balloons.

name: Lithium
fact: Light enough to float on water, it powers the rechargeable batteries in your devices.

name: Beryllium
fact: Stiff and feather-light, it is used in aerospace alloys and is nearly transparent to X-rays.

name: Boron
fact: A metalloid used in heat-proof borosilicate glass and in super-strong magnets.

name: Carbon
fact: The backbone of life; it forms diamond, graphite and more compounds than any other element.

name: Nitrogen
fact: About 78% of the air you breathe; liquid nitrogen boils at a frosty -196°C.

name: Oxygen
fact: About 21% of the air and essential for both breathing and burning.

name: Fluorine
fact: The most reactive element of all — it even attacks noble gases — and it fights cavities in toothpaste.

name: Neon
fact: Its glowing orange-red light gave the world the classic neon sign.

name: Sodium
fact: A soft metal that fizzes violently in water; with chlorine it becomes ordinary table salt.

name: Magnesium
fact: Burns with a blinding white flame and sits at the heart of every chlorophyll molecule.

name: Aluminium
fact: The most abundant metal in Earth's crust — light, rust-proof and endlessly recyclable.

name: Silicon
fact: The second most abundant element in the crust and the brains of every computer chip.

name: Phosphorus
fact: White phosphorus glows in the dark; your DNA, ATP and bones all depend on it.

name: Sulfur
fact: Bright yellow and famous for the rotten-egg smell of its compound hydrogen sulfide.

name: Chlorine
fact: A yellow-green gas that disinfects drinking water and becomes PVC plastic.

name: Argon
fact: The most common noble gas in air; it fills light bulbs and shields welding arcs.

name: Potassium
fact: Vital for nerve impulses and muscle function — bananas are a famously modest source.

name: Calcium
fact: Sturdy bones — and snail shells — are built from this most abundant metal in the human body.

name: Scandium
fact: A rare, light metal that toughens aluminium alloys and brightens stadium lamps.

name: Titanium
fact: Strong, light and rust-proof, it goes into jet aircraft, dental implants and white paint.

name: Vanadium
fact: A few percent of it makes steel dramatically stronger; its compounds are vividly colourful.

name: Chromium
fact: Gives stainless steel its shine and rubies their deep red glow.

name: Manganese
fact: Hardens steel and enables photosynthesis by splitting water in plants.

name: Iron
fact: The most used metal on Earth and the atom that lets hemoglobin carry oxygen in your blood.

name: Cobalt
fact: Paints glass deep blue and keeps lithium batteries from overheating.

name: Nickel
fact: Rust-resistant and magnetic; it gives coins their shine and adds toughness to steel.

name: Copper
fact: A superb conductor that has been used for millennia and naturally kills bacteria.

name: Zinc
fact: Sacrifices itself to protect steel from rust and drives hundreds of enzymes in your body.

name: Gallium
fact: Melts in your hand at 30°C and glows inside blue LEDs.

name: Germanium
fact: A metalloid that guides light through fibre-optic cables and sees in infrared.

name: Arsenic
fact: A notorious poison that also makes the semiconductor gallium arsenide.

name: Selenium
fact: Powers old photocopiers, treats dandruff and is a tiny but vital nutrient.

name: Bromine
fact: One of only two elements that are liquid at room temperature; it slows flames in plastics.

name: Krypton
fact: A noble gas that creates brilliant white camera flashes.

name: Rubidium
fact: Its atoms keep ultra-precise time in atomic clocks and see in the dark in night-vision gear.

name: Strontium
fact: Burns brilliant red — the colour behind countless fireworks displays.

name: Yttrium
fact: A hidden helper in LEDs, superconductors and cancer-fighting microspheres.

name: Zirconium
fact: Nearly invisible to neutrons, it clads nuclear fuel rods; as cubic zirconia it fakes diamonds.

name: Niobium
fact: Becomes superconducting when cold and strengthens MRI magnets and jet engines.

name: Molybdenum
fact: Toughens steel and helps plants and bacteria pull nitrogen from the air.

name: Technetium
fact: The first element made by humans; Tc-99m lights up millions of medical scans.

name: Ruthenium
fact: A tough, rare metal that hardens electrical contacts and wear-resistant alloys.

name: Rhodium
fact: Often the most expensive metal on Earth; it scrubs car exhaust clean.

name: Palladium
fact: Soaks up huge volumes of hydrogen and cleans car exhaust as a catalyst.

name: Silver
fact: The best electrical and thermal conductor of any element.

name: Cadmium
fact: A toxic metal behind bright yellow pigments and old rechargeable batteries.

name: Indium
fact: Its oxide makes touchscreens both transparent and electrically conductive.

name: Tin
fact: The metal that turns copper into bronze and electronics into solder joints.

name: Antimony
fact: A flame retardant and ancient eye cosmetic; it also hardens lead alloys.

name: Tellurium
fact: Rarer than platinum in Earth's crust and a key layer in thin-film solar panels.

name: Iodine
fact: A purple-vapour halogen used as an antiseptic and needed by your thyroid gland.

name: Xenon
fact: Ion thrusters push spacecraft with it, it lights car headlights and even works as an anaesthetic.

name: Caesium
fact: The most reactive metal, and the atom whose vibration defines the second.

name: Barium
fact: Paints fireworks green and lets doctors X-ray the digestive tract.

name: Lanthanum
fact: Improves camera lenses and sits in the electrodes of NiMH batteries.

name: Cerium
fact: The most abundant rare earth — it sparks lighter flints and self-cleans ovens.

name: Praseodymium
fact: Tints welders' goggles yellow-green and boosts powerful magnets.

name: Neodymium
fact: Its magnets are the strongest made, powering earbuds, motors and wind turbines.

name: Promethium
fact: Radioactive and vanishingly rare; it once lit glow-in-the-dark dials and powers tiny nuclear batteries.

name: Samarium
fact: Keeps magnets working at blistering temperatures; Sm-153 relieves cancer pain.

name: Europium
fact: Gives banknotes their glowing red security marks and old TVs their red glow.

name: Gadolinium
fact: Extremely magnetic — it sharpens MRI images as a contrast agent.

name: Terbium
fact: Glows green in displays and keeps neodymium magnets strong when hot.

name: Dysprosium
fact: Its name means 'hard to get'; it keeps EV motor magnets working under heat.

name: Holmium
fact: Has one of the strongest magnetic moments of any atom and cuts tissue in surgical lasers.

name: Erbium
fact: Boosts light pulses in fibre-optic cables and tints glass rose-pink.

name: Thulium
fact: The rarest natural lanthanide; a portable X-ray source in a thimble.

name: Ytterbium
fact: Ticks inside the world's most precise optical clocks and strengthens stainless steel.

name: Lutetium
fact: The densest, hardest lanthanide; its crystals catch gamma rays in PET scanners.

name: Hafnium
fact: Gulps down neutrons in reactor control rods and insulates the newest transistors.

name: Tantalum
fact: Ignored by body fluids, it anchors surgical implants and packs huge charge into tiny capacitors.

name: Tungsten
fact: Holds the record for the highest melting point of any metal: 3422°C.

name: Rhenium
fact: One of the rarest elements on Earth and a superalloy secret of jet engines.

name: Osmium
fact: The densest naturally occurring element — a golf-ball-sized chunk would weigh about a kilogram.

name: Iridium
fact: A thin worldwide layer of it marks the asteroid impact that ended the dinosaurs.

name: Platinum
fact: Precious, unreactive and a superb catalyst in cars and chemical plants.

name: Gold
fact: So unreactive it never tarnishes; it coats astronaut visors and backs bank vaults.

name: Mercury
fact: The only metal that is liquid at room temperature — and dangerously toxic.

name: Thallium
fact: Odourless, tasteless and deadly; once sold as rat poison, today used in infrared optics.

name: Lead
fact: Dense enough to block radiation, yet a potent poison for nerves and brains.

name: Bismuth
fact: Grows rainbow staircase crystals and is technically radioactive — but only just.

name: Polonium
fact: Discovered by Marie Curie and named for Poland; a speck of it packs lethal radioactivity.

name: Astatine
fact: The rarest natural element on Earth — probably less than 30 grams exists in the crust.

name: Radon
fact: A radioactive gas seeping from soil; the second leading cause of lung cancer.

name: Francium
fact: The most unstable natural element — less than 30 g exists on Earth at any moment.

name: Radium
fact: Once painted on glowing watch dials, with deadly consequences for the workers.

name: Actinium
fact: Glows an eerie blue in the dark and is being tested in targeted cancer therapy.

name: Thorium
fact: A possible future nuclear fuel, four times more abundant than uranium.

name: Protactinium
fact: A rare, radioactive metal studied for future nuclear fuel cycles.

name: Uranium
fact: Its U-235 nuclei split in chains, powering reactors and lighting cities.

name: Neptunium
fact: The first element beyond uranium, now used in neutron detectors.

name: Plutonium
fact: Its heat powers the probes now leaving the solar system.

name: Americium
fact: A speck of it sits inside most smoke detectors, spotting fires before they spread.

name: Curium
fact: Named for the Curies and carried on Mars rovers to read alien rocks.

name: Berkelium
fact: Named after Berkeley, California; its atoms helped forge element 117.

name: Californium
fact: A fierce neutron source used to kick-start reactors and hunt for gold ore.

name: Einsteinium
fact: First found in the fallout of a hydrogen-bomb test; named after Einstein.

name: Fermium
fact: Named after Enrico Fermi and created only in explosions or accelerators.

name: Mendelevium
fact: Named after Mendeleev, the chemist who first arranged this table.

name: Nobelium
fact: Named after Alfred Nobel; its chemistry is still a near-total mystery.

name: Lawrencium
fact: Named for cyclotron inventor Ernest Lawrence; the final actinide.

name: Rutherfordium
fact: Named after Ernest Rutherford, the father of nuclear physics.

name: Dubnium
fact: Named after Dubna, Russia, home of a legendary nuclear lab.

name: Seaborgium
fact: Named after Glenn Seaborg, who helped create many elements beyond uranium.

name: Bohrium
fact: Named after Niels Bohr; its atoms survive only seconds.

name: Hassium
fact: Named after Hesse, Germany; possibly the densest element ever created.

name: Meitnerium
fact: Named after Lise Meitner, who explained nuclear fission.

name: Darmstadtium
fact: Forged one atom at a time in Darmstadt, Germany — home of this element.

name: Roentgenium
fact: Named after Wilhelm Röntgen, who took the first X-ray.

name: Copernicium
fact: Named after Copernicus; theories suggest it may behave like a gas.

name: Nihonium
fact: The first element discovered in Japan, from 'Nihon' — Land of the Rising Sun.

name: Flerovium
fact: Named after the Flerov Laboratory; it may act like a noble gas.

name: Moscovium
fact: Named for the Moscow region; only single atoms have ever existed.

name: Livermorium
fact: Named after the Lawrence Livermore laboratory in California.

name: Tennessine
fact: Named after Tennessee and the heaviest halogen known.

name: Oganesson
fact: The heaviest element known; it defies its noble-gas column and is expected to be a solid.
